subtopic: TEESWATER, ONT.  CONSTRUCTION OF NEW POST OFFICE
speechtext:
The Minister of National Defence this morning has revived the discussion of the estimates of this department which were started late in June. I suppose because of the fact that there has been such a long intermission from the start of these estimates to the present time there will be a certain prolongation of the discussion. It is unfortunate that we cannot start a department like this and carry on for three or four days in order to complete it all at once.
I do not wish to repeat arguments or statements that have been advanced by other hon. members but I would like to say a few words in general consideration of the policy of the Department of National Defence. I notice in the white paper and in the earlier statement of the minister that Canada's objectives in national defence remain the same concerning the defence of Canada, our commitments under the NATO alliance and our obligations, if any, under the United Nations. There has been no change from the past several years but nevertheless the world situation has altered rather materially and li' wonder whether the minister and his officials have taken that fully into account.
Other people have drawn attention to the fact that the estimates for this year do not vary by a dollar from the estimates for last year' It is a little surprising in view of the necessity for making a reappraisal of the

world situation each year. It is again a bit surprising in view of the action taken by other countries within the NATO alliance with regard to their defence expenditures.
I would have thought there would have been some change in the total amount made available for national defence. Surely it is not just a revolving fund that is going to remain unchanged from year to year.
There must be some alteration one way or another when one recalls that it is only a few years ago, in 1950, I think it was, that our expenditures for national defence were running at about $435 million; and then with the outbreak of war in Korea and with the necessity of assisting our allies under NATO and the necessity for stockpiling and preparing for a possible third world war the estimates for national defence jumped and have remained at a high figure from that time forward. They are now in the neighbourhood of $1,775 million.
From the minister's statement of several weeks ago and his statement today I am not clear that his appreciation of the world situation is the same as that expressed by other people charged with similar responsibilities in other countries. The impression I get from reading magazine articles and newspapers with regard to defence thinking in other countries is that the threat of a thermonuclear war, a third world war, has diminished but that we still have to take precautions and not let our guard down, but nevertheless I do not see that world opinion considers that a third world war is imminent at the present time.
On the other hand I gather that anyone who is thinking of warfare is of the opinion that if trouble breaks out again it will be of a limited nature and conventional arms will be used. Under those circumstances the policy of the Department of National Defence must be rather nicely balanced.
We as a country are not in a position to enter into competition in the development of thermonuclear weapons. We have to be dependent upon our more powerful allies. We apparently are not in a position to do very much in regard to the development of missiles and there again we must be dependent upon those who have greater financial resources and who are ahead of us in experimentation. I wonder if it would not be wise for Canada to place a greater reliance upon our larger allies in these matters and perhaps give our attention to other matters.
The minister has pointed out that it is worth while developing a team of experts who will have some knowledge of the construction of missiles. That is all right as far as it

goes, but perhaps greater reliance should be placed upon those other countries who have gone further in that field. There is nothing to prevent the Department of National Defence of this country from keeping well up to date and in a fine state of efficiency the three fighting services as we have known them in the past, and keeping them supplied with the necessary modern equipment for the type of warfare that has been carried on since the second world war.
I think it is an open question as to whether that is being done. I feel we have not yet received an adequate answer from the minister with regard to the great amount of money that has been expended over the last five or six years in strengthening our defences. We are not yet assured that we have forces in being ready to take action on short notice either in this country or elsewhere. We are not yet assured that air transport is adequate to lift a substantial portion of the army. We are not yet assured from the standpoint of mobility that the army is equipped in modern fashion so that it can be not only transported but supplied by means of air.
And yet what has happened to all the money that has been spent over the last half dozen years? I have no objection to the development of a camp such as Gagetown.
We saw the necessity for that at the time of the Korean war when our troops had to go into the United States to receive their training. I have no objection to the better facilities which are now available for service personnel at the various stations across Canada; that is all right. We have raised no serious objection to the stockpiling of equipment which was the major point of policy a few years ago. However, some of those things must surely have been completed now, and throughout it all there is a doubt as to whether our forces in being are capable of immediate action. That may be true of the air force which is stationed in Germany; it may be true of the air force in Canada; it may also be true of the naval forces, although they are not complete. But I wonder if it is true with regard to the army? The minister has not cleared up that point. The difficulty in discussing defence estimates is that the curtain of secrecy descends just about every other second and you cannot get a great deal of information.
I noticed that in his opening remarks on June 20 the minister referred to what he described as a major change within the army. This is a matter which we have discussed from this side of the house on many occasions. It is a matter concerning which I was rather critical of the minister last year. I refer to the substantial increase in the armoured corps within the Canadian army. This
Supply-National Defence is indeed a concession to opposition criticism and is an acknowledgment of the existence of modern thinking with regard to balanced forces within the army. The minister has told us that a third armoured regiment is to be activated. He did not say when; he did not name the regiment and he did not notify us whether the three armoured regiments which would then be under command would be brigaded or whether they would simply operate as independent units.
I was glad to discover that the minister had arrived at a conclusion that something should be done with regard to a subject which I have discussed so many times in the house, the armoured personnel carrier, the finest protection for the infantry soldier that has been brought about in modern times. I should like to quote the words of the minister as reported on page 5212 of Hansard of June 20 as follows:
Another important new development on which the army is working is an armoured amphibious 9-ton tracked carrier.
This will be capable of mounting field guns or of moving 10 or 12 infantry men and will be resistant to small arms fire and to splinters from shell fire. The minister stated that the army was working on this development. I do not know whether that means it is just drawing up plans, whether this vehicle is on the production line or whether it is in use. We shall certainly watch with interest the development of vehicles of this nature. Last year we were informed that the army was watching with interest the development of vehicles of this nature in the British and United States armies, but that is as far as that information went. I think the minister might very well give us information later on as to how far this development has gone. I certainly welcome it and am glad to hear that our authorities are going to make provision for the protection of the infantry along such a well tried line.
I would draw the attention of the committee-to the fact that in the army being developed! in West Germany there is a marked emphasis on armour. In the NATO letter of January 1, 1956, at page 13, reference is made to the 12 divisions which will comprise the German army as follows:
Half of the twelve divisions will be armoured divisions while the remaining six will be grenadier divisions, that is to say fully mechanized infantry divisions (as far as possible on tracked vehicles) with strong armoured support.
Profiting from their experience in the last war and being now able to start afresh with their special sagacity in military matters, the Germans are balancing their army most carefully as between armour and infantry and are planning to have the infantry in tracked

Supply-National Defence carriers, thereby creating mobility to move across the country and not be tied down to roads as the army was in the second world war.
The Germans are particularly efficient in military matters, as they have shown in the past. When they plan an army on that basis I think it is well worth the attention of Canada. Our army should be planned along similar lines with sufficient armour to balance the infantry forces which should be in position where they can achieve mobility with protection and to permit crossing the country which can be done only with tracked armoured vehicles. I would hope that in the exercises now being conducted at Gagetown some emphasis will be placed on this_ method of using the infantry and that the'tactical exercises being conducted there will utilize the experience of the past and be in line with modern developments.
In connection with the general over-all allocation of funds, the minister has discovered that he requires the same amount of money this year as he sought in past years. Although he has made changes up and down within the various groupings in the Department of National Defence, the grand total remains the same. I notice that in making any reductions that are made the axe is used on the army to the extent of $24 million.
I wonder why the army was selected as the service which should have to suffer this reduction. If there was to be an over-all reduction perhaps each service should have been affected. If it was to be a temporary re-allocation of funds so that the research end could be supported, as happens in this case because they get this money, why do not the other two services make contributions toward that end? But no, it is the army which has to bear the brunt of this change to the extent of $24 million.
In any war in the immediate future which is not a world war the army will play a major part. It played a major part in Korea. A recent publication of the historical section gives the story of Canada's army in Korea and indicates that of Canada's 1,557 battle casualties, all but 14 were suffered by the army. The air force participated in that war by supplying a certain number of pilots to the United States air force and by using its transport squadrons to ship supplies and men overseas. The navy participated in Korean waters, but the brunt fell upon the army. In any war similar to Korea the brunt will again fall on the army. So I wonder why in effecting reductions the minister should select the army as the place where they will be made.
What will it mean? The minister might tell us what it will mean to the army. Is it [Mr. Churchill.l
going to mean something different in the way of equipment? Will there be a shortage of guns or transport? Will there be delay in providing tanks for the newly activated armoured regiment? Will there be a delay in providing these specially designed armoured personnel carriers? Something will have to be curtailed in so far as the army is concerned. Yet, if trouble breaks out as it did in Korea, and the decision has to be arrived at within 24 hours or within a week, I am sure that it will be the army that will be called upon to play its part, because none of these wars are fought solely by navies and air forces. The army has to get in there on the ground. The experience of Korea is an indication that the air force alone cannot win a war. Air superiority was enjoyed by the United Nations forces in Korea, and yet the North Koreans and the Chinese were able to bring that war virtually to a stalemate. In the closing year of the second world war in Europe, although we enjoyed air superiority, the Germans were able to put up very effective defensive operations.
So we cannot be dependent just on air, and certainly not just on the navy. We come back finally to the army. The army has to be there and has to take over, run the risks and endure the casualties. The army must be kept in as good a state as either of the other services. I wonder whether that is in the plan of the minister as regards this reduction he has proposed this year.
There is another point. I should like to know from the minister whether he has been drawing upon the experience of the past in order to make the army a more effective fighting instrument. Perhaps the minister has heard sufficient-he may hear more- with regard to the criticism offered against his department by recently retired generals. I have here a publication by Major General Burns dealing with manpower in the Canadian army, a very fine study of the situation that prevailed in world war II concerning the utilization of manpower by the Canadian army. I wonder whether the minister has given attention to that and whether the present forces of the Canadian army are built up with the experience of the second world war in mind, as brought to our attention by Major General Burns.
He points out in his study that in his opinion about 6 per cent of the strength of the Canadian army in Europe in world war II could have been utilized-or saved, as he puts it-for fighting purposes, that is, in his opinion, far too many of our troops were engaged in the rear areas and in administration and on staff, and more should have been available for the fighting edge or

fringe of the army. He makes a comparison with other forces in that war and indicates that in the Canadian set-up we exceeded the British and the United States forces in the number of people that we had behind the lines in the supply line, in the administrative echelons and so on. If his conclusions are correct, that lesson should be applied to the formation of the Canadian army at the present time.
What is the effective fighting strength of the Canadian army now? Are there too many people behind that fighting edge? Is it top-heavy in the wrong places? I do not know; I have not had a chance to check Major General Burns' figures against those of other nations, but he is of the opinion that percentagewise the Canadians had far too many men in the pipe line. I hardly like to use that word nowadays, but in wartime it was used to indicate those who were coming along from the depots and so on up to the front. It may be that we have not profited by the lessons of the second world war and still have too many people back of the fighting fringe; and it is the fighting fringe that is the important element. Perhaps at Gagetown, where the troops are now assembled, there may be more men in the rear areas than there should be. I should like to hear what the minister's comments would be with regard to that.
I do not wish to prolong this aspect of the discussion, Mr. Chairman, but in general I think that the Department of National Defence faces a tremendous problem. We admit that. Although we feel it is necessary to offer criticism of that department, we recognize the tremendous problem involved. We recognize the fact that the department has to keep in mind two types of warfare, the third world war with thermonuclear weapons and the brush-fire type of war where conventional weapons will be used. We recognize the fact that more importance is being attached to air than was the case years ago, and so on. Nevertheless a department which is utilizing about 40 per cent of the taxes collected by the dominion government must he submitted to close scrutiny, and I think an accurate accounting of the use of all this money is certainly required.
From my standpoint, the vital factor is whether or not we have efficient forces that are capable of being used immediately they are required. We cannot overlook the fact that in 1950, when the Korean war broke out, we were not prepared to send a force to Korea and had hastily to assemble a large number of men, and there was a great deal of wastage. To keep 8,000 men enlisted, well -over 10,000 had to be brought in even before
Supply-National Defence the brigade sailed for Korea; and 1,500 were discharged because they were unsuitable for active service; they should never have been taken in. Is that type of wasteful use of manpower going to occur in the future, or what protection have we against that?
That is the type of criticism that I think should be aimed at the Department of National Defence. There should be a strict accounting of the use of all this money that is available, to indicate to us that we are enjoying the protection we want and that we are able to take part at any time we are required to do so under our commitments with regard to NATO or the United Nations.

subtopic: TEESWATER, ONT.  CONSTRUCTION OF NEW POST OFFICE
speechtext:
I was glad that the minister took time at the beginning of the discussion today to reply to some of the comments that had been made when his department was last before the house. In those remarks he made one or two references to me, particularly on the subject of my comments concerning the importance of Canada's radar screen. I was glad to see that on that point there was some degree of agreement in regard to this important subject. However, whilst he quoted with some degree of relish my remarks in that regard, I think he still failed to get the point I raised when I was referring to the importance of the radar screen. At page 5266 of Hansard of June 21, I concluded my discussion of that subject with this statement:
Therefore I am one of those who believe that the radar installations are a very necessary and important development in any comprehensive program of air defence at this time.
I should like to stress the words "in any comprehensive program of air defence at this time". I still agree with that statement, namely that in a comprehensive air defence program it is imperative at the present stage of air power development that we have a radar screen capable of giving sufficient advance warning to make it possible for the United States strategic bomber air force to carry out its role of massive retaliation and to make it possible for the Canadian air force to carry out its major role of defence of the North American continent. However, he did not include the proviso that I have made to the effect that I did not feel that, at the present stage of development, Canada had a comprehensive air defence program nor, for that matter, an over-all clear-cut comprehensive defence program generally. If we are to put my statement in the proper perspective, I think it is necessary to include that proviso.
The minister stated further, Mr. Chairman, that in making my observations the other day, I seemed to have a fair degree of information,

Supply-National Defence and he suggested that that fact more or less rebutted complaint that we in this house lack sufficient information to deal intelligently or adequately with the discussion of defence matters generally. Last year I think I complimented the minister. He had just taken over the department, and I think I complimented the minister on a change in emphasis in so far as this particular problem was concerned. I suggested that the minister had been more free with his information and that statement was true at the time. But as he has acquired experience in the office, he seems to have been returning to the former policy of reticence which makes it extremely difficult for the private member in this house to have an adequate grasp of defence matters. It is because of that fact that I would agree heartily with the suggestion of the Leader of the Opposition that we need a committee that can discuss matters of defence which, by their very nature, tend to be concerned with a classified kind of information, and thereby put ourselves properly and adequately into the picture. If I seem to have any grasp of the problem at all I would suggest, Mr. Chairman, that it is largely as a result of information that I have been able to acquire owing to my own service experience, and particularly by examining the more detailed information that is available from United States sources. If it were possible for a private member in this house to read and to analyse carefully the information, for example, that is placed on record before the various hearings in the United States, we would be completely informed on defence matters. However, with all the other responsibilities resting on us, time does not make it possible to carry out that exhaustive analysis. We are able to get only the highlights of those discussions from the publications that appear from time to time. Those publications have largely been the source of my information on the general problems relating to air defence in Canada and air defence in North America.
Having dealt with those two particular references by the minister to my previous remarks, I want to carry on with a subject that I was not able to deal with the other day because of lack of time. One of the deficiencies in our air defence program as well as in our defence program generally relates to manpower. As I said in my closing remarks on June 21, I want to make some reference to the subject of the utilization of reserves and auxiliary personnel in the Royal Canadian Air Force. Back about four or five years ago, before we had any fully operational permanent air force squadrons available for the defence of Canada, the idea used to be put forward that the auxiliary squadrons were our front line of defence and
IMr. Dinsdale.l
that they were sufficiently well trained and that their numbers were sufficiently large to assure an adequate defence of Canada and this continent from any possible approach from the north.
I can remember taking issue with that thesis at the time. Others from relatively high level sources in the auxiliary also disagreed with the thesis. I think Wing Commander Rohmer of Toronto, for example, disagreed rather heartily in a public statement with that particular theory. By reason of the obsolete equipment supplied to our auxiliary squadrons, it was not possible for them to cope with any challenge that might come to this continent at that time. This year quite obviously the minister agrees that we were a little bit overoptimistic in those days concerning the ability of the auxiliary and reserve units adequately to defend this country. But unfortunately the pendulum seems to be swinging too far the other way, and there is now a tendency to underestimate completely the ability of the auxiliary units of the air force to serve in any defensive capacity. For example, in his initial statement the minister gave us the information that a general reorganization of our auxiliary units was under way, and that reorganization included the disbanding of 424 squadron and the reassignment of 420 squadron in London to new duties as was announced at the opening of today's sitting. Further, it has been announced that the participation of auxiliary flying units in actual defensive combat is to be strictly limited. I feel, Mr. Chairman, that that is carrying the reaction much too far to the other extreme. From the information I have and from the personal contact I have had with auxiliary work, I am quite prepared to state that our auxiliary units are in a position to cope with any kind of defensive role to which they may be assigned in this country.
Before world war II I remember there was a lot of criticism concerning the functions of the university squadrons that were operating in the United Kingdom. At that time they were the backbone of a numerically very weak air power. It was felt that the types of aircraft were advanced in those days at least; the Hurricane and Spitfire were much too complicated and hot for the week-end university squadron fliers to cope with. As it turned out, during the battle of Britain these so-called week-end fliers became the first few who met the first onslaught of the formidable German luftwaffe. Some of our thinking from that period has carried over into the post world war II period, and we have the idea that advance jet aircraft are much too complicated to be coped with by part-time fliers on a week-end basis.

It seems to me, from the information I have been able to glean, that is not the heart of the difficulty. It is not a lack of qualified aircrew personnel, both pilots and navigators, which makes it difficult for our reserve units to continue operational in their defensive role, but rather it is a shortage of ground and maintenance personnel. It is very difficult to get reserve auxiliary people to put in the necessary time to keep themselves up to operational requirements on a short-term basis. If that is the difficulty, I am sure the recent action taken by the Department of Defence, as announced by the minister in this house, to reorganize the role of auxiliaries is not going to contribute in any positive way to the solution of that problem. Rather, the abrupt manner in which No. 424 squadron is being disbanded peremptorily, and it would seem without any preliminary warning, is going to have a further detrimental effect on morale and esprit de corps amongst auxiliary personnel.
I was surprised, speaking just for a moment to the difficulty faced by No. 424 squadron at Hamilton, at the degree of protest that was generated by this rather arbitrary action. For instance, in the eleven o'clock T.V. news roundup on C.B.C. they showed rather extensive pictures of a parade of protest that had been organized by the citizens of Hamilton because of this rather high-handed action on the part of the defence department. Now, that aroused my curiosity and I made some inquiries as to the reason for this enthusiastic response. I had it confirmed that the squadron was all prepared for its period of summer training. The majority of the squadron personnel had made arrangements to get leave of absence from their various businesses for the period. They had had no preliminary warning at all that flying operations were going to be discontinued. They had had an outstanding record, as incidentally have all auxiliary squadrons, with reference to safety. They have had, I understand, an accident-free flying record, which is an exceptional record when we consider the accident rate even in the best trained civilian aviation circles.
Furthermore, I understand that all the flying personnel were operational on T-33 jet type aircraft. Enthusiasm was high, morale was high, esprit de corps was high. They were a model auxiliary squadron, prepared to move into action immediately in the defence of the vital Hamilton industrial area. Suddenly, without warning, without previous contemplation, they found themselves abolished. Now, that is hardly the type of action that is going to overcome the reluctance that is manifest from time to time in getting Canadian civilians to spend time as part-time fliers or maintenance personnel in auxiliary
Supply-National Defence squadrons. It is very bad for morale. If we have had difficulty in the past in keeping auxiliary maintenance personnel up to strength, that problem will only be aggravated by this particular action.
Now, other than the experience of No. 424 squadron, I have had some personal experience down through the past five or six years in this matter of serving in auxiliary or reserve capacity. I have brought this subject up year after year. We have an active air force association in my city of Brandon, an air force association that has repeatedly taken honours because of its enthusiastic participation in the activities of the air force association of this country. Recently, I received from that association a circular which was rather disconcerting. This group of veterans who have since the end of the war been trying to find a niche in Canada's defence scheme of things in an auxiliary have, in all instances, been turned down. I have recited the procedure before. They hoped to have an auxiliary flying unit in the first instance. Then, they moved to the ground observers corps. Then, they hoped to have a radar light warning unit, but in each case, according to official information, there was no possible niche into which they could fit in the auxiliary scheme of things. However, they continued to thrive largely as a social club. You can only continue to operate on that basis successfully for so long, and now the interest is waning. The circular was in the form of a questionnaire asking a couple of hundred members of the association whether they considered it worthwhile to continue as an organized unit. I mention that again because it seems to fit into the general attitude which has been felt towards the role and function of auxiliary units in Canada. I think the attitude towards No. 424 squadron has been outstanding in this respect.
Let me be somewhat more positive regarding auxiliary functions. One of the most worth-while projects of the department has been the M.A.T.P., mobilization assignment training program. On April 24, in answer to a question, I received the information that since the inauguration of this scheme in 1951 the officer personnel serving under the M.A.T.P. plan, that is understudying permanent officers in various roles in the air force, have increased from 78 in 1951-52 to a total of 481 in 1955-56. There was a slight decrease in figures, as a matter of fact there was a decrease of some 14 in the number serving from 1954-55 to 1955-56. Therefore, I would take it from these figures the minister and the department concluded that this is a very worth-while project.

Supply-National Defence
Let me turn to the N.C.O.'s scheme of things. Here again is where we have difficulty with maintenance personnel. Your maintenance personnel are going to be drawn largely from the N.C.O. ranks. I believe it was in 1954-55 that the scheme was first opened to senior N.C.O.'s and in that year 60 served, but in 1955-56 the total went down to 57. We are not doing so well in interesting the N.C.O.'s in this worth-while auxiliary service capacity. I do not know where the problem is there, but I do believe that because of the tremendous expense involved in supporting a large enough air force in Canada to carry out our primary defence role, the difficulty that we have been having is obvious. All that is necessary is to look at the newspapers that almost plead for our young people to become interested in serving Canada. The bands of the air force are busy all year round visiting high schools in an attempt to interest our young Canadians in a career in the air force, and yet we seem to ignore the most fruitful source of manpower, and that is the underlying interest of the veterans in serving in an auxiliary capacity. As I said in the opening part of my remarks, I feel that the auxiliary branch of the air force, if the proper approach is made by the department, is capable of serving in every way in the various parts of Canada's defence operations.
There is one specific point that might be raised which could probably explain the lack of interest of N.C.O.'s as well as the decline, so far as officers are concerned, indicated in the past two years. No way has as yet been devised whereby both officers and N.C.O.'s serving in the M.A.T.P. scheme can receive promotion. I have raised this problem before. It is not uncommon, for example, to find a flying officer understudying a squadron leader. He is learning the job that in the permanent force is handled by a squadron leader of the permanent force. This flying officer returns year after year, four, five or six years, to understudy the squadron leader, and so far as he is concerned that is the highest level to which he can rise in the air force scheme of things. There is absolutely no incentive from a promotional standpoint.
During the war when a man served as a wartime member of the air force and occupied a certain position he was elevated to the acting rank of that particular position. When he no longer functioned in that capacity he was demoted to what they called their substantive rank. I feel it might be a further source of incentive for officers, and particularly for N.C.O.'s, if it could be made possible for them, as they accumulate experience in the air service, to move gradually
fMr. Dinsdale.]
toward the equivalent rank that they are understudying. There is more than the status of rank involved, there is also the difference in pay; and when you are taking time off voluntarily from your civilian occupation- and in a good many cases civilians do not have a long enough holiday period to cover the basic 15 days required in this type of service-it would be a relatively inexpensive way of bringing the strength of the air force personnel up to the numbers required to carry out adequately Canada's defensive role. On this point, Mr. Chairman, I think our civil service is the worst offender so far as making it possible for members of the civil service to obtain leave of absence to serve in a reserve or an auxiliary capacity is concerned. I have bumped into this complaint specifically from acquaintances I have in the civil service. If the minister makes an inquiry he will find that it is extremely difficult for a civil servant to get the necessary time off to serve his country in this additional way, and certainly the public service should be the first in establishing the pattern, in setting the example for private employers and private industry.
This is all I have to say on the auxiliary and on the reserve at this time. I feel it is one of the deficiencies in a comprehensive air defence policy in Canada. It is fine to have an expensive radar screen spanning the continent at three levels, but it remains only as a Maginot line unless you have the personnel, the aircraft and the other aspects of defence necessary to carry out an adequate air defence role.

subtopic: TEESWATER, ONT.  CONSTRUCTION OF NEW POST OFFICE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this matter of national defence is a most complicated field, probably the one in which greater doubts can be expressed and questions raised than in almost any other field with which members of parliament have to deal. And, certainly, one is not speaking with any professional knowledge of the subject when one attempts to speak this afternoon. Any experience that I had was in a war many, many years ago, whose practices and weapons have been completely outmoded.
However, I do not feel too bad about dealing with this matter at this time because I understand the minister himself in his opening speech-and I think quite properly- admitted and said-and perhaps this is one of the more encouraging things that we have found from the minister's approach to his department-that he himself did not know the answers to many of the problems with which he was confronted, and he felt quite certain it would be a long time before all the answers were given. With that I quite

agree. In approaching the matter this afternoon, Mr. Chairman, I am doing it in that spirit, not in one of criticism as such except perhaps on one particular approach; that is, I feel that because of this doubt, because of the uncertainties, the request that has been made by this party, and particularly by the Leader of the Opposition, that the whole matter should be referred to a committee for investigation, is entirely justified, although I realize it cannot be done at this session at this late hour. Anything I do say about these problems I hope will be directed toward the end that in another year that will be done.
The problem of war is very different now from what it was at one time. Originally, I suppose, people went to war to get food and possibly to get slaves; some tribes went to war to get wives, and gradually they went to war to capture land. Wars were therefore at one time profitable, or at least our ancestors must have thought so.
I remember a former speaker of this house, the late Mr. Rhodes, telling me once of a trip he made to Britain during the first world war. While he was there he was entertained at a luncheon by the Vickers Armstrong Company, I think it was, the great armament manufacturers. During the course of the luncheon he said he assumed they had solved all the problems with which they were confronted and they said, "No, we have only one problem with which we still have to deal, and that is to find a shell that will pierce the strongest armour plate and conversely find an armoured plate that will resist any shell."
I presume that problem is still with us. Perhaps, however, it does not have to be solved today, because I suppose you could have the strongest armour plate in the world; but a battleship with the greatest thickness of armour plate cruising the seas does not have to be struck by a shell. A bomb bursting 5,000 feet or more above it, or perhaps several miles away, could reduce the armour plate to scrap and everyone within the ship to a burnt crisp in a matter of seconds.
We have reached the stage, Mr. Chairman, where one sometimes wonders if these discussions concerning war are-I will not say archaic, but are hardly realistic in one sense of the word. We have all heard a great deal of talk about whether we are going to have a brush fire war or an all-out war. Who is going to draw the line between a brush fire war and an all-out war? I do not think anyone can answer that question. For instance, if Hitler had had a thermonuclear weapon in the latter part of the last war and had realized he was losing the war, who would
Supply-National Defence question the fact that he would not have hesitated to use it even though there might have been an understanding at the beginning of the war that it would not be used?
We talked a great deal about the other side not using gas in the last war, but to a large extent that was perhaps a tactical weapon. I am sure that in the last few days of the war Hitler would not have hesitated to use gas if he had felt that by doing so the war could have been won. I do not think there is any real value in our hoping that certain weapons will not be used, nor in our hoping that we will have a brush fire or a conventional war rather than an all-out war. One can start off with that hope and with that plan, but when one side realizes it is losing the war and hopes that by using some other weapons the loss of that war can be avoided, I think one can expect that such weapons will be used.
The ultimate aim of all these things, of course, as the minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs realize, is to create a state of disarmament wherein there can be some real hope that neither brush fire nor thermonuclear warfare will be engaged in at all. I think what we have to do in the meantime until that situation develops is to work out some modus vivendi whereby we can maintain our own way of life and stand prepared to defend ourselves against an attack should it come. That, of course, as the minister said, constitutes the problem with which we are confronted.
The hon. -member for Brandon-Souris in justifying the expenditures on radar lines a few moments ago said that after all

and this is a point which I think the general public does not appreciate-their real purpose is to give the strategic air command a chance to get its planes off the ground. Their purpose is not to protect the public, as I understand it, but is rather to give the bombers a chance to get into the air so they will not be destroyed on the ground and in order that they can launch a counter measure of massive retaliation about which we have sometimes heard in the past. Well, if that is the hope and the only hope to be derived from them it does not hold out much comfort for the rest of us, because we are probably going to be burnt to a crisp anyway. If we reach that stage of crisis where we are under attack and are launching a retaliatory attack, the world will be in that state that has been caricatured by a monkey scrambling over the rocks overlooking the devastated countryside and commenting to himself that no one should ever start this foolishness all over again.
We do not want to go that far, yet apparently that is the degree of desperation

Supply-National Defence to which we are forced when we talk about these radar lines. Several hundred years ago when our ancestors came to this country they erected stockades and withdrew behind them every night. Then gradually they spread out over this continent and the pax Britannica spread over the world. We had several centuries on this continent and one century as far as the world was concerned of prosperity and relative peace. At least any wars that occurred were on a tribal basis.
I sometimes wonder if we are reverting to the stockade mentality in this country, withdrawing behind the stockades of the radar lines in North America as our ancestor withdrew behind their stockades in order to protect themselves from Indian attacks. The only thing which occurs to me in this connection is that perhaps the stockades which protected our ancestors against the Indians were more effective than the stockades we are erecting on this continent today.
When I come up to this house in the morning and return at night I cross the Rideau canal, and it is forcibly impressed upon me that it was the distant early warning line of the past because we were then guarding ourselves against attacks that might have been launched against us from the south. We know from our reading of history that the canal was built from Ottawa to Kingston in order that we could move our troops into the great lakes and ward off an attack from the aggressor which would come from the south.
That D.E.W. line, if I might call it that, may have served a useful purpose; it may have protected us against aggression, I do not know. I really doubt it. Nevertheless it certainly involved the expenditure of terrific sums of money in those days which may have been all to the good in expanding the gross national product. It undoubtedly serves a useful purpose today because it is now one of the beauty spots of Ottawa, and young boys and girls can paddle up and down there at night in canoes and whisper sweet nothings and make love to one another. It therefore really serves a tremendously useful purpose.
I sometimes wonder if the radar lines in the north will ever serve a useful purpose. It is not possible to sit on them and hold hands and whisper sweet nothings. I have been informed that it is too cold up there, even for the birds to do that, so I wonder whether the expenditure for the stockade of today will have the same justification as the expenditure which was made for this D.E.W. line of a great many years ago. In any event, we are told it is necessary as a part of our defence machinery, and there is

a great deal one has to accept on faith. I presume the statement of the experts to that effect falls into this category.
But there is one thing one learns in this country, and I suppose in any country, and that is that it is advisable to know what the public are saying. I think generally we who believe in the democratic system, although we may violently disagree with the results that are sometimes expressed, also believe that the verdict of the people is something that has merit and something to which one should listen. I think the trouble with a good many people today is that they cannot listen. If you go into the average home you will find the television set blaring and you are not able to have a conversation. If you travel on a plane you find that it travels at such a vast speed and makes so much noise that it is impossible to be heard by your travelling companion and it is equally impossible to listen to him.
I prefer to travel by train and take it leisurely. If one does that one can sit in the club car or the smoking lounge and talk to people and listen to them, and one can learn what the average businessman and the ordinary citizen of this country are thinking. There are many of these ordinary Canadian citizens who wonder just what justification there is for the expenditure of millions of dollars on the various radar lines. We hear of hundreds of millions of dollars being paid out for all this, yet in the next breath we hear that the I.C.B.M. will be developed within a few years. Apparently all we have to learn is how to bring it down from the air without it burning up, and how to make it hit its target. If we can do that we will have mastered everything and will have a weapon capable of blasting us into kingdom come.
The minister told us that he thought that weapon was further removed than the columnists seemed to suggest. I hope he is right. However, I do not think anyone expects, and I do not think the Secretary of State for External Affairs will suggest, that there is any danger or likelihood of war breaking out in the immediate future, a conventional war with planes and all the rest of it. At any rate these questions are being raised by the public. They know that something must be done and no one is particularly critical, yet there is that reserve of doubt which is increasing as time goes along.
That is not good. Apparently we are in for a long-term pull in this world in which we now live. We have seen the difficulties which the secretary of state and his associates have had in trying to work out even an approach to disarmament. We hear of the evasions, the

committees, the adjournments, the postponements and I am sure the utter frustration that comes from it all. The fact is that we have to maintain a high degree of preparedness and defence for many years to come. To do that we must have a spirit of acceptance by the Canadian people and the public generally. No one is going to refuse for one moment to pay out money if it is necessary and if the expenditures are justified, but sometimes there is the thought that perhaps we are living in two worlds. At one moment we are told that war is an impossibility, then at the same time we are asked to prepare for war.
We have heard a great deal in this country about co-operation among ourselves and other countries. The public are becoming a little alarmed about this. We do not seem to be able to even co-operate on the manufacture of our rifle. I think there must be a greater degree of co-operation, of mutual trust and of working together than anything which has been indicated in the past. This morning the minister told us, I think in answer to a question, that we had spent $24 million on the "Pussy Willow" or the "Velvet Glove" or the "Puss in Boots", whatever it is, this mysterious weapon which we tried to develop and then had to drop.
There is some question as to the degree to which a country such as ours should embark upon scientific work of that kind unless we are assured that there has been close study, that this work is closely integrated with that of other countries, and that they are prepared to co-operate. One country should not try to take more credit than it deserves because of national pride or the ambition of someone to carry out work which should be spread more evenly across the board.
From what the minister has said, from this expenditure of $24 million we at least got some negative benefit or perhaps constructive benefit, in that we found out how it could not be done. That is quite a high price to pay for such negative results. It reminds me of the college mathematics professor who stood up before his class and put a great many algebraic and geometric designs on the blackboard. Finally he stood back and scratched his head. One of the students asked him what that proved. The professor replied, "My boy, that proves we cannot do it that way." If that is all we got from the $24 million expenditure it may be hard to justify it.
The unfortunate part, and here one can be more critical, is that quite often it has been necessary to go to the records of the United States in order to get information on these things. I believe the minister was sincere when he said this morning that he had never
Supply-National Defence refused to answer a question, that he had given all the information it was possible to give. He even convinced me at the moment that he believed that statement when he made it. But certainly the newspaper editors of this country do not believe that. They do not doubt the minister's word per se, but they certainly doubt that we can get the necessary information. Members of parliament do not believe that. We do not get the information we want. It is impossible in a bulky committee of 175 members, or whatever the number is, in a short period of three or five days-

After all there are four other committees sitting at the moment, which makes it all the harder for one to explore these matters and get the background and the, shall I say, philosophic approach to the problems with which the department is confronted. I suggest that that cannot be done in a committee of this kind in the short time which is available to us. It is just utter nonsense to think it can be done.
The minister may say that he has given us all the information he can and all the information for which we have asked, but that is not the case. Since the Korean war and up to the end of this year we will have spent in Canada over $10 billion on national defence. I venture to suggest that the great majority of Canadians know much more about the Einstein theory of relativity than they do about how the Department of National Defence spent that amount of money during the last few years.
Year after year we were denied information because it was classified, particularly by the minister's predecessor; yet the Leader of the Opposition spent 15 minutes one day reading into the record evidence given before a Senate committee of the United States where everything which had been denied to us as being classified was exposed. Only lately we had a general from the United States air department giving criticism of the CF-100, our inadequate radar screen and all the rest of it. Unfortunately it seems that we can get more information from the proceedings of a committee of the United States Senate than we can from our own department.
I could go on giving illustration after illustration, but I do not propose to take the time of the committee to do so. I simply want to say again that I believe and I think we all believe we are in a long, long period of tension during which this country and other freedom-loving countries will have to
6138	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence spend much more money than they want to spend. They will have to do it in order to preserve their freedom. If you are to do that you must have an educated and instructed public opinion to give you its support.
There are many ways in which the communist menace can be met, and I do not think it is going to be done by picket lines. I do not think it is going to be done by bayonets alone. It has to be done in other ways. We have to maintain our financial strength. We have to maintain public opinion. We have to have the zeal, the determination and the belief that we are doing the right thing and that we are working together toward the right end.
We read what is written by perhaps a fifth columnist; we read what is written by experienced newspapermen like Norman Smith or by industrialists like James Duncan; but whichever way you turn you read how the Russians are working with zeal, with determination and with interest which everyone suggests puts us to shame. If we are going to work as we should, I say again that we have to mobilize public opinion as much as we have to mobilize our manpower.
I think one way in which that can be done is by the setting up of a defence committee such as has been urged by the Leader of the Opposition.
As I said earlier, I know it cannot be done at this' late hour in the session if it is to serve a useful purpose, unless it is allowed to sit after the housg rises, but I suggest that the minister take this suggestion seriously. When this house reconvenes next year, whenever that may be, he owes it to the Canadian people and he owes it to himself that there should be a full and searching inquiry into all these matters to which I have made vague references this afternoon.
We know that the one key to our survival is that we have the power to defend ourselves, to retaliate, to deter others from acts of aggression because we have the power to strike back if they strike us. We are in the unfortunate position, with our way of life, that we have to sit back and be prepared yet not take any aggressive steps ourselves. That requires a great deal of thought and development of the proper approach psychologically and socially in a nation. As I said before, and I do not wish to repeat myself, one way in which that can be done is by the appointment of this committee. I certainly believe that should be done when this parliament reconvenes.

subtopic: TEESWATER, ONT.  CONSTRUCTION OF NEW POST OFFICE
speechtext:
At the outset I should like to endorse wholeheartedly the remarks of the previous speaker. I think he hit the nail fMr. Nowlan.]	!

on the head when he spoke of the need for public opinion and the determination of the people not only of Canada but of any nation to defend themselves and equip themselves for that defence.
A few days ago, when these estimates were previously before the house, our leader, the hon. member for Peace River, spoke of the struggle being waged to spread communism throughout the world and the battle between two great ideologies. I think all of us agree that this has divided the world into two great camps of which the dividing lines are constantly changing. In a state of fear, the democracies are spending billions of dollars to put themselves in a position for the defence, not only of themselves but of all friendly peoples, against the military might of the nations behind the iron curtain. These nations seem determined that the ideology of communism shall prevail not only in their own countries but shall spread throughout the world.
Today this small nation of 16 million people is faced with estimates of $lf billion for the purpose of defending itself against this threat, and we in this parliament are properly quite concerned. We do not begrudge the money, and we are certainly in accord with the first sentence of the white paper:
The aim of Canada's defence program and planning is to provide for the security of Canada.
We agree with that wholeheartedly. We have read this white paper through quite carefully and we are in agreement with the ideas expressed therein. I do not believe there is a single Canadian who will question the fact that it should be the aim of Canada to provide a program and plan of defence for the security of Canada; but the time has passed when we must accept these estimates blindly. I agree with every speaker who has spoken thus far and suggested that these estimates and the whole problem of defence should go before a committee on defence.
I believe this committee should be permanent and should be sitting not necessarily only while the house is in session but as need arises throughout the year. The Leader of the Opposition made a moving demand for such action, and I am sure the thinking members of this house will support that demand.
The minister himself expressed the wish that we should ask questions so he could add to the information he has already given in his speech and in the white paper, but how can we ask questions when there is nothing concrete placed before us on which to base our questions? What facts have been given to us? Are we still at the stage where we are put off with the old eyewash that it is not in the national interest to make these

things public? I claim that the only enemy we can think of at the present time knows more about our military defences than any member of this house, and I am not excepting the Minister of National Defence himself. Since coming to this house I have been made to feel that I would be disloyal if I questioned these estimates in any way, but I believe the day for that type of thinking is passed. The time has now come to get down to brass tacks and study in a businesslike manner the expenditures with which we are faced.
There is one thing we ask, and I think it is the important thing in the minds of most people. Are we getting value for the dollars being spent? The people of Canada have a right to know the answer, and we as their representatives have a right to get that answer for them. We want facts, not literary gems as we were handed in the white paper.
I refer to paragraph 6, wherein we are told:
Canada's principal support of the west's retaliatory striking power is our contribution towards early warning and air defence on this continent.
I should like you to visualize a map of Canada showing these warning lines on which we have spent so much money. We have the <'Pinetree" system, the mid-Canada supplementary warning line and the distant early warning line. When we see these on the map we are lulled into what may be a false sense of security. I know that the defence department feels justified in having these lines and in feeling that it is the only way to provide what they hope these warning lines will provide. But we read articles in our press and periodicals, supposedly by experts, who tell us that these lines are obsolete. What are we to do? Whom should we believe?
There I think is another reason why we should have the opportunity of calling these experts before a committee and getting the facts. Millions have been spent on these lines. I hope they have been wisely spent, and I hope the plan to continue to spend many more millions will also be wise. But, on the other hand, if it should be proven that those lines are obsolete, why continue spending millions of dollars of our taxpayers' money on this system of defence? The taxpayers would certainly like to know.
Then in paragraph 7 we speak of our navy and the defence of our sea lanes. The minister recognizes our responsibility with respect to the naval service, but is recognition enough? In the same white paper, at page 6, we see a listing of our naval strength. It looks very imposing and I hope it is very effective. However, we should like to be assured by naval experts that the strength and the composition of our navy will allow
Supply-National Defence it to do the job that will be required under conditions that will exist in a future war.
Then we come down to paragraph 9, which reads in part as follows:
9. As a result of the build-up in defence strength and organization during the past several years, Canada's armed forces are now more effective than ever before in our peace-time history.
That is certainly good news, Mr. Chairman; but then is it enough? It is not a question of whether these may be more effective than they have ever been before in our peacetime history. The question is whether they are effective in comparison with what we know is the standard today in the nations that may be our enemies tomorrow. That is the kind of information we want to get. Experts who profess to know something of the science of modern warfare contend that we lag far behind. I am not going to stand up here and put forward any opinion as to who is right or who is wrong. However, I would still say that we want to know the facts, and that the only way in which to get those facts is to have these experts before a committee set up to study the whole problem.
There is a controversy over the mobility of our forces and there is also a controversy in the old country at the present time over the same problem. I notice that there is a difference of opinion as to whether we should have fluid mobility on the ground or whether our defensive troops should be airborne. We see that the trend is toward airborne troops, and I am personally inclined to believe that that is the proper procedure. But then, in the light of the fact that experts have said it is unwise to neglect ground mobility, I would say that we should again ask ourselves the question, are we neglecting ground mobility for airborne mobility?
I am perfectly satisfied that, with regard to getting into the northern areas of Canada, we have not the roads by which we could transport troops. Instead of depending on air mobility, might not the smart thing be to build access roads into those areas? I can quite agree that if troops were landed by an enemy power in those parts of Canada, once they had occupied their position on the ground, in any attempt to meet that threat by means of airborne strength our forces would certainly be at a great disadvantage in landing, especially when within reach of an enemy who was already settled in those areas. Hence it may be that ground mobility still has a large place in the make-up and in the consideration of providing defence for our remote areas.
Of course there is another reason why we should have a committee, namely to get the
6140	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence considered findings of the experts who should know. We are not questioning the ability of any official of the Department of National Defence. I hope the plans that are being followed are the best plans that the brains and the know-how of our people can provide. But I believe that all doubt raised in our minds by these noted authorities not only in Canada but in the United States and Great Britain should be cleared away; and again I would say that the only way to do that is by means of a committee of this house.
I now come back to the first sentence in this white paper:
1. The aim of Canada's defence program and planning is to provide for the security of Canada.
The whole emphasis is on military defence, but I just wonder whether that is the allimportant thing in connection with the problems which we we are facing today. The only enemy, of course, we have in mind is Russia and the iron curtain countries, but I sometimes wonder whether it is just wise to concentrate on warfare conducted entirely in a military manner. We think of world war III, the war about which we talk so much and hope will never happen. We visualize a rain of devastating destruction delivered by the Russians, something which may never happen yet could happen.
I say, Mr. Chairman, that we have been at war. This world war III has been going on for some years. In fact it has been going on ever since the communist leaders decided to spread their doctrines throughout the world. You can call it world war III, the cold war or the battle for men's minds- it makes no difference what you call it -but as yet there has been no clash of the armed forces and so far our defences are geared entirely to meet that clash that we are expecting to happen.
Yet there have been battles. We do not like to say that they have been wars. We like to refer to them as incidents. There has been the Korean incident. There has been the incident in Indo-China. There has been the incident in Morocco. There have been the Israeli-Arab border clashes. We have the Algeria incident, and we have the Cyprus incident. All this is similar to what was happening before the actual world war II broke out in full force. As you will remember, before that happened we had the Ethiopian incident and we had the Saar valley incident. They were similar to the incidents that are taking place in the world at the present time.
Then after world war II was actually under way in earnest, you will remember the months that the German army stood motionless before the Maginot line. You


heard and read of the phony war. We could not understand what was going on or what was taking place. Yet actually what was going on? The same thing was going on at that time, Mr. Chairman, as is going on today. The nazis were no more idle than are the communists in this day and age. The nazis were softening the enemy from within. When this had been done, what happened? The German juggernaut rolled on into France almost without opposition. Laval and his gang had softened qr had broken down the French people's will to resist, the will to defend themselves. Then we had Quisling in Norway.
I do not blame the local people or do not pretend to say that Quisling and Laval were set up there at the wishes of the Norwegian and the French people. These traitors, Mr. Chairman, were put there and encouraged to gain control of their people by the nazi agents, just the same as we have communist agents working in the various countries of the world today. This gives us something to think about. We do not like to even suspect that there may be a Quisling in Canada or in any of the other free nations of the world, but then who would ever have thought there would be a Quisling in Norway, a country we knew for generations as one of the most democratic and freedom-loving? Yet Quisling came to the front in Norway. The same thing could happen here. We have planning and scheming to weaken our people from within and to destroy our determination to stand for individual freedom and to defend our democratic way of life. In this struggle, Mr. Chairman, we can ask ourselves, will communism survive or will freedom prevail?
In this struggle I have mentioned these are incidents or steps in the greatest battle the world has ever known. There will be more leading up to the final clash. If it comes it will mean the obliteration of one of the great forces in the world. Will it be communism or democracy that survives? That is the question that thinking men and women of the free nations of the world are asking themselves as they look into the future. If the armed clash never comes it will be the greatest victory the free world has ever known. If it never comes it will mean that the communists know they have lost the battle for men's minds. It will mean that Canada and the other free nations have provided for their security, not by military preparedness but, as the hon. member who just spoke mentioned, by building up the determination and the will of the peoples Of the free world to defend themselves against communism on the home front.

Communism, Mr. Chairman, is the enemy against which we must defend ourselves. It cannot be done with armies, ships and planes. It must be done by education, by leadership, by giving our people and all the free peoples of the world, as well as those people who would like to be free, a way of life and ideals that communism cannot give. That is the answer to communism both from without and within. It cannot be done by any one department. It cannot be done by the department of defence. It cannot be done by the government of Canada. But I will say that it can be done by all the governments and all the free nations co-operating in a plan to give the free peoples everywhere something better to live for, and something better to die for if need be. It will not be an easy struggle. It will take billions, but I am satisfied that the free world including the people of Canada will not be averse to spend their billions if they see they are winning in this fight against communism.

speechtext:
Speaking earlier this morning, Mr. Chairman, the Minister of National Defence said he felt he had given all the explanations for which he had been asked, with one or two limited exceptions which he listed, and that he found it rather hard to understand why members criticized him or his department on the basis of being unable to get full information about national defence policy and activities. There is one outstanding matter for which I do not believe the minister will contend for a moment he has given adequate explanation or information, and that is the fact that the total asked in the estimates for national defence this year is dollar for dollar with the amount asked for last year, notwithstanding that there is in this country a large body of opinion which feels that our defence program should be substantially revised, and notwithstanding that in other major western countries there have already been substantial revisions of the defence program.
We have had nothing in the way of an adequate answer to the criticisms that have been made of the old look of Canada's defence program and of the concrete suggestions that have been made for revising and altering the character and composition of our defence program so we might have a new, up to date look with respect to our defence efforts. It is within that general framework of inability to get concrete, down to earth discussion of defence policy that the detailed criticism arises of the minister and his department for not furnishing adequate information. It is because of that sense of frustration, if you will, resulting from the inadequacy of the discussions and answers which are given
Supply-National Defence here, that the demand for a committee on defence estimates has arisen. We have not had an adequate answer from the minister as to why that demand should not be met. It met with a substantial body of support in the press and from other informed critics in Canada. We have not had an adequate reply from the department.
It is also in that framework that I want to make certain criticisms of the department and of certain things which have taken place. It may be said that these incidents to which I shall refer are in themselves minor matters; at least of some of them that might be said. I am quite prepared to admit that one or two of them are small matters, primarily of local significance. However, the only explanation I can find for the incidents to which I shall refer is that the policy of the department and the minister's grasp of the department lack cohesion and lack a central co-ordination. It is the multiplication of this sort of incident which gives rise to the general criticism and the feeling that until we get some adequate method of discussing and coming to grips with defence policy, we shall not be able to improve the situation.
Reference was made earlier to certain unsatisfactory conditions with respect to civilian employees of the department. The minister in reply this morning told us that the Department of Labour carries out an annual study of the prevailing rates of wages in areas where the department employs casual or prevailing rates employees, and an attempt is made to keep the scales of pay of those employees of the department in conformity with the prevailing rates in the area. Well, we accept the minister's word for that, but I do not know why it is that there is so much dissatisfaction and such discrepancy between the rates paid to civilians in the department and those paid in comparable civilian employment in the area itself. I have annually, some cases more than annually, complaints from the employees of the naval ammunitions depot near my own city, particularly from the fire-fighting personnel in that depot. They had facts which they laid before me and which I passed on to the department, and they certainly substantiate their claim that they are not in receipt of remuneration comparable with that received by those in similar employment in strictly civilian capacities in that area.
Just recently I have had correspondence with the minister with regard to the situation at the former No. 37 ordnance ammunition depot at Kamloops, particularly with respect to the provision of fire-fighting personnel to protect that depot. There exists here a state of absolute confusion, confusion

Supply-National Defence confounded, as I shall indicate to the minister by his own replies to me which are apparently at variance with what the department itself is doing there with respect to the employment of fire-fighting personnel.
We had three ammunition depots at Kamloops, a naval depot, an army ordnance ammunition depot and an air force depot. It was recently decided to close down the air force depot and move the personnel and I believe the ammunition to Edmonton, and that the army ordnance personnel should take over the air force depot. That move has now been completed and the former ordnance depot-that is the magazines and the physical installations-are no longer manned on a full-time basis by the ordnance corps personnel. I should of course observe that each of these ammunition depots naturally enough requires not only civilian guardians but adequately trained fire-fighting personnel ready at a moment's notice to deal with an outbreak of fire, should it take place. The situation is that the fire-fighting personnel formerly in charge of the work at the ordnance depot have been moved out to the former air force depot which the ordnance has taken over; but in the magazines of the former ordnance depot there is stored, and I am told will be stored permanently a very substantial amount of ammunition, though the personnel by and large have all been moved out to an area at least some 12 miles from where the former ordnance depot is. All that is left at the old depot to protect the magazines full of ammunition are five guards who are on a 24-hour basis, which means that there are three in the day watch, one in the evening watch and one at night.
I should point out to the committee that those magazines are near a growing area which was first built up by the Veterans Land Act authorities. It is just outside the city limits, and beyond it lies this Veterans Land Act settlement where there are now, I should think, at least 150 families and, as you will appreciate, Mr. Chairman, families in the nature of things with an increasing number of young children. I am told that the experience of the guards there has been that on an average of three times a week they have found those young children wandering about and getting into the area of the magazine. You will appreciate the concern that causes the parents, when they know that large quantities of ammunition are stored under what I submit definitely is inadequate care, and in an area back in the hills where children are in the habit of wandering about.
I brought this matter to the attention of the minister because I learned that the firefighting personnel previously in charge of
IMr. Fulton.]
these physical establishments had been laid off during the period of the move, and those at the former air force depot were now being laid off. Upon learning that and also upon learning of the concern felt by the residents of the district for the safety of their children and their own homes, I got in touch with the minister on June 18 and outlined the situation to him, and asked him a question in the house on June 20. In reply to that question the minister said, as recorded at page 5206 of Hansard:
I have looked Into the situation and according to the advice I have received there is a permanent staff of five civilian watchmen at No. 37 ammunition depot at Kamloops. They are all well-trained in fire prevention methods as laid down by the Royal Canadian Ordance Corps regulations. In addition, of course, the navy has a fire-fighting detachment on the other side of Kamloops which is on duty in three shifts 24 hours a day and is therefore always available.
I do not know whether or not the minister has been given the full information, though I would hope he would make it his own concern to get it because, as I told him, this is a matter of very great concern to the people of that district. The answer that there are five civilian watchmen at the depot gives a wrong impression. There are five there, yes; but they are, as I say, on three shifts. There are three during the main daylight watch, but in the two other watches there is only one to guard an area of a score or more of acres, if my impression is correct. There is only one telephone at the old entrance to the camp, and this one man, when there is one man on duty, has to make a tour of the area. If he should find any trouble he may be a matter of half a mile or a mile away from the telephone. When he is there all alone it would take him a matter of some minutes, at any rate, if not an appreciable number of minutes, to get back to the telephone and get word to anyone to come to render any assistance. This one man could not do anything with respect to fighting a fire, should a fire break out.
The minister says there is a naval firefighting staff. They are some three miles on the other side of the city. They would have to go right through the city to get there, and it seems to me to be courting disaster to say that a fire brigade which is still necessary on the basis of a constant 24-hour watch at the naval depot is going to be relied upon to travel about two miles, and then one mile through the city of Kamloops, and half a mile on the other side of the city and then deal with a fire out there. How long does the minister think it would be before men could be got to it, and what would happen to the naval depot in the

meantime? Yet the minister apparently has been told, according to what he said to me, that his department thinks that adequate safeguards, adequate care and fire protection, are available at the old naval ammunition depot. He went on to explain the situation with regard to what I had told him in these words:
I think probably what the hon. member refers to is that recently there was a fairly large amount of ammunition supplies being transferred to the [DOT]depot at Rayleigh.
That is the former air force depot which the army took over. I continue:
A number of civilians were engaged on a temporary basis to assist in this movement and to ensure safe handling. They were classified as watchmen or fire-fighters. When the transfer was complete they were released.
Well, X have written the minister again since this question and answer took place, pointing out to him some of the facts I have laid before him and before the committee, and I pointed out to him that it was an odd thing that he would tell me on June 20 that a number of these personnel had been released, notwithstanding what I had told him as to the necessity of fire-fighters at this former depot. Yet I have in my hand a poster put out by the civil service commission of Canada dated Vancouver, British Columbia, June 15, reading as follows:
Civil Service of Canada Requires Fire-fighters-
Department of National Defence-
Kamloops, B.C.
On the one hand the department tells me on June 20 these men were laid off because their services were no longer required, and on June 15 the same department puts out a poster advertising for fire-fighters.
