Some of them were, but my information is that others who are now without work were certainly involved-I am not able to say whether or not they were definitely classified in this way-and were performing the duties of fire-fighters before the move and during the time the move took place.
There is a twofold difficulty that the magazines not now in active use but in which a large quantity of ammunition is stored are without adequate guard and without adequate fire-fighting protection; these men have been laid off, and at the same time the civil service advertised for fire-fighters for the Department of National Defence at Kamloops.
I would ask the minister now to look into the situation himself and find out what are the facts. I am confident if that is done he will agree with me there is a need for another look at the situation. I believe there is some conflict of opinion in his own department concerning the matter. I believe that if he investigates the matter and gets to the bottom of it he will agree with me there is a confused and unsatisfactory situation in this connection.
I would also like to refer to another situation which is causing concern to the people of Canada, and that is in connection with the radar line installations. I have a twofold criticism here, both a general one and a particular one. We are very much concerned both over what Canada is spending on these radar lines from the point of view of whether we are getting value for the money. Others have discussed that and I do not need to deal in any detail with that problem. We are also concerned as to whether Canada has in fact parted with its sovereignty particularly with respect to the D.E.W. line, and to a lesser extent in connection with the "Pinetree" line, and whether the basis upon which the handing over of the installation and the manning of these lines to the United States was justified.
In this connection I would refer the committee to a thoughtful though critical article by Mr. Ralph Allen, the editor of Maclean's magazine, in the May 26 issue, entitled "Will D.E.W. line cost Canada its northland?" On page 17 of that issue of Maclean's, referring to the D.E.W. line installation, Mr. Allen said this:
It is the charter under which a tenth of Canada may very well become the world's most northerly banana republic. For a sum of money that has been officially estimated at four hundred million

Supply-National Defence
dollars we have at least temporarily traded off our whole northern frontier. In law we still own this northern frontier. In fact we do not.
In the illustration on page 17 the approximate locations of the three lines are traced out and the following wording appears:
D.E.W. line, cost $400 million. United States pays all.
Mid-Canada line, cost $170 million. Canada pays all.
Pinetree line, cost $450 million. United States pays two thirds.
Judging from many of these articles and other comments I have heard and read the justification for the situation on the D.E.W. line is that it is of primary benefit to the United States. It is going to cost $400 million; therefore it is only fair that the United States who wanted it built as a crash program should pay for it. I have also seen suggestions to the effect that it is extremely questionable whether Canada had either the physical resources to build it or the trained and skilled personnel to man it, and therefore it is said again it is quite appropriate to have the United States build and man it on the basis they are doing.
Mr. Allen has some interesting comments on that aspect of the matter at page 69 of his article. This article is based, I should say, on a personal tour he made under arrangements made by our defence department and that of the United States government, in conjunction with a number of other newsmen. He says:
In return for the luxury of not spending money on the D.E.W. line we Canadians have surrendered something that for the last generation we have regarded as our greatest necessity: our independence. For a sum of money that during the approximate construction period of D.E.W. line- roughly 1954 to 1957-will be somewhat more than equalled by the taxes we will pay on tobacco, we have delegated the effective working control of at least 10 per cent of our land area to the United States air force.
Mr. Allen makes a sincere and conscientious effort to be fair about this, and he does pay tribute to the United States personnel who are manning these installations and those in charge of them at United States headquarters for their concerted effort not to be irritating to Canadians and to do everything possible to avoid any personal breaches or anything which would give rise to a feeling on the part of the Canadians that the Americans are in fact bossing the situation up there. He does point out, however, that the existence of the situation makes such a feeling inevitable despite how conscientiously the Americans may try to avoid it, and he gives these examples of the feeling that has been engendered.
The following incident occurred on the way up to the R.C.A.F. station at Frobisher
[Mr Fulton.]
bay on Baffin island. In referring to the incident on page 70 the author says:
Later the station commander explained the exact division of functions on the base between the U.S. and Canadian air forces. "The USAF," he said, "is responsible for administration and operations. The R.C.A.F. is responsible for policy." Walking back to the mess, I asked a fellow reporter what he made of these distinctions. "It's easy", he said. "If you want to fly airplanes around here, you ask Washington. If you want to open a saloon you ask Ottawa."
A little later on he says:
But no amount of rough-hewn, new-world courtesy can conceal from anyone the simple facts that our basic allegiances-
He was referring to the two allegiances as between Canada and the United States.
-though nearly parallel, are not exactly so and that a good and loyal Canadian and a good and loyal American are not necessarily good and loyal in precisely the same manners and directions.
I am going to quote at some length from this because it is a revealing article. He refers to the feeling which is engendered as between Canadians and Americans out of the D.E.W. line and the inevitable feeling of annoyance which comes to Canadians. I continue:
In this confusion and mistrust there may lie unsuspected threats to the shadow of Canadian dominion over the Canadian north. The substance has already begun to disappear.
The most experienced and responsible Canadian I met in the north was a man I'd rather not identify more closely than that. I asked him bluntly: "Do you and your friends resent the presence of the Americans here?" "No," he said sadly, "it's the other way around. They resent our presence here."
Then he sums it up as follows:
How many dollars equal how much independence? How much independence have we really lost and how much of it could we have saved? How much more will be lost as our comfortable acceptance of the presence here of U.S. military commanders, U.S. military troops and U.S. military installations becomes as naturally ingrained as our acceptance of U.S. business capital and U.S. television, books and movies. To make any comparison, however remote, between what a few Canadian NATO squadrons might mean to the national identity of France and what a U.S. military base 2,500 miles long within Canada's geographical limits might mean to the national identity of Canada is to invoke one of the largest and sickest red herrings in the history of debate.
Under the original agreement Canada still has the right to take over the operation of D.E.W. line on "reasonable notice". To do so might represent a decline in the quality of our bookkeeping but there are good reasons to believe it would also represent an improvement in the quality cf our statesmanship.
That is the sort of situation which makes Canadians question the policies of the Canadian government with respect to national defence the way we intend to defend our country, to do our part in defending Canada, as we say we do from time to time, according to the statements of the minister in the house

and as contained in the white paper. The question is whether this money we are spending is being spent wisely and efficiently.
The other experiences which have occurred in connection with these radar installations give rise to the same outlook. These experiences have to do with the readiness of the department to hide its actions under the cloak of security considerations. It is disturbing to the Canadian people to learn that these things are being built, and they want to find what they are being built for and how much they are costing. You cannot get that information because of the so-called security.
I should like to relate a couple of experiences I had which reinforce this feeling. There is a radar installation in the northern part of my riding. I am quite certain that its location is known not only to our potential enemy but to hundreds of my own constituents. It was supposed to be a secret. Suddenly a large number of United States service personnel began to move into the area with bulldozers, trucks and other equipment. Contractors began to move around and considerable construction took place at a point some 60 miles from the nearest substantial centre of population.
I was up visiting this area one day and found people waiting for me at the hotel. They wanted to know what they could do about getting compensation from the government for the damage they had suffered because of the construction of this radar station. I told them there was not much point in my trying to obtain anything because I knew nothing about it. They asked me if I did not know that the United States was building a big radar station at a point which I shall call X. I told them I knew they were building a radar line, but I did not know the exact location. I told them that when I went back I would take it up with the department. I was given the details of the damage suffered.
The minister's predecessor was then in charge of the department, and when I came back I outlined this situation to him in as strong language as I could use and still be polite. I told him I felt it was absolute folly that the last person to learn of the installation of a radar station in a constituency should be the member who represented that constituency. I said that a member should not be jplaced in the position of going up to an area and having people ask him how they would go about getting compensation, and having to say that he did not know the station was there.
I pointed out to the then minister, as I point out to the present minister, that these things cannot be kept secret. You cannot instal a radar station and bring in Americans
Supply-National Defence with all their construction equipment and keep it a secret. Members of parliament, whether on the opposition side or the government side, should be in a position to be of assistance to the department in smoothing the way for the installation of these things, in smoothing the settlement of claims and in explaining to their people who are annoyed at what is going on, that the installation is necessary and justified. A member should be in the position of being able to assist the department in explaining these things to those who from time to time are resentful and critical.
The minister of that day agreed. He said he felt that was a reasonable point of view, that perhaps it was not wise that these things should be kept secret from members, especially when knowledge of them was bound to become widespread.
Recently I was taking my family home for the summer, and after spending two or three days in Kamloops I returned to Ottawa. At that time I was not making any extensive tour, but my next door neighbour asked me about the radar station that was being constructed up at a place he named not very far north of Kamloops. He told me that United States servicemen were moving in in large numbers. I said that I thought this was the same old story, that this was supposed to be a security matter and I asked him what he knew about it. He told me that they could not find out very much about it, as they were told it was secret. But some United States servicemen had come in along with construction machinery. This was all taking place on a favourite ski slope, but the area was fenced off and they could not get in there. Yet no one was supposed to know anything about it. You go home and you have your neighbours asking you about these things and you have to give the foolish answer that it is a security matter and members of parliament cannot be told about it; and all this notwithstanding the conversation I had with the minister's predecessor, when I thought the point had been established.
On the way back to Ottawa on the train I picked up the Winnipeg Free Press at Winnipeg as I always do, which contained the following article:

Kamloops, B.C. (CP)-Four Vancouver men. on a top-secret survey mission for the federal government, died Wednesday in the unexplained crash of their amphibian aircraft.
A transport department investigation has been ordered.
Carl J. Baxter has been identified as the pilot. Also aboard were Don McVeigh, a construction superintendent and Ron Grierson, both employees of Bennett and White Construction Co. Ltd., of Vancouver.

The fourth man was identified as W. J. Sckyra of Defence Construction, Ltd., a crown corporation operated by the Department of Defence Production.
The plane, a twin-engine Grumman Widgeon, was owned by Bennett and White but company officials declined comment on the nature of the survey, stating:
"It is classified-we can't tell you everything."
The article said "everything" but I think they should have said "anything" because that is the attitude of the department. In a later press story I saw that the crash had taken place on the mountain near Kamloops on which this radar installation was being made. How absolutely ridiculous it is. Not only are we not told in this house the particulars of the cost and purposes of these things, we are told that we cannot even be told where they are located. We go home and are asked by our constituents about it, and we are the last people to find out about it. Then an airplane crash takes place practically on the site, and it is reported in the press, but they say, "We still cannot say anything about it or what is going on up there." We are not able to get information when United States servicemen are being brought into the area and say, as they have in the past on occasion said to our Canadian con-situents, "You can't come in here, bud; this is security." We are told this is all supposed to be secret, that these things are to be installed and the Americans are manning them.
No wonder the Canadian people are critical of the attitude of the department and the way it spends their money, and no wonder members of parliament are unable to do anything but agree with the Canadian people in that attitude. I feel no false personal pride as a member of parliament. I am only saying that because I am a member of parliament I should be told, because one of the things that members are for is to obtain knowledge on behalf of their constituents of what goes on. What the government overlooks so often, it seems to me, is that members of parliament have a right to know and that the people also have a right to expect their members to be informed so they can tell them what is going on, and so the members can exercise their proper function of ensuring that the people's money is spent wisely and that the people are getting value for that money.

Four or five decades ago wars were small operations engaged in by a few professional troops. War itself was probably looked upon as an extension of diplomacy. It was something to be used where diplomatic methods failed. Up to the first world war, the nations of the world had war departments as departments of government. Then, with the last two world wars, people began to realize that wars were no longer something engaged in only by a few professionals. They were no longer matters that were not the concern of the whole population, because a modern war required the efforts of the whole population and could be a national catastrophe. Then it became the custom to call certain departments of the government "departments of defence" or "departments of national defence". War departments became defence departments.
Since the second world war there has been a great acceleration in this evolution. It may or may not have been progress, but in any case we in this age find ourselves in an entirely new set of circumstances. It is my contention that under the present circumstances what we need in reality is not a department of defence but a department of survival or, better still, a whole segment of government which in close co-operation and co-ordination tries to discover a means whereby we as a people and as a nation can survive.
I am deeply worried by the fact that, instead of that, we seem to have not even a government with certain departments concerned directly or indirectly with defence but a government made up of compartments which should together be concerned with defence, compartments which see their own problems and try to meet them conscientiously but without seeing the significance of the over-all picture. This set-up reminds me of the six blind men of Indostan, who went to see an elephant so they-

Now that the senior member for Halifax has finished, I shall continue. We have the situation where the Department of National Defence is carrying on programs, I think conscientiously, trying to meet the problems of defence as it sees them from a professional soldier's point of view. We have the Department of Defence Production claiming that it has no concern except to supply what the Department of National Defence requires, regardless of whether or not it makes sense from a production point of view. As a result of that, we also have the Department of Defence Production doing most of its producing in our large cosmopolitan areas. The result is that our large cities are growing larger every day, and to house the growing number of workers congregated in these areas we have the Minister of Public Works helping to build more houses in these congested areas. From there the problem is tossed to the Minister of National Health and Welfare, who is responsible for the matter of civil defence. These problems are being created by one department to be solved by another.
We have the situation that our cities have become so large and congested that it would be impossible, or at least impractical, to evacuate them in case of an atomic attack. That is why I likened the situation to the six blind men of Indostan. The minister of defence could be likened to the second of the six:
The second, feeling of the tusk,
Cried, "Ho! what have we here So very round and smooth and sharp?
To me 'tis mighty clear This wonder of an elephant Is very like a spear!"
That illustrates in a homely way the situation of defence if you look at it only from the point of view of professional soldiers. There was a fifth man also, the one who happened to grope against the ear, but to save the minister embarrassment I shall not mention him further.
I say this not in a spirit of ridicule or of jest but because I think it is a suitable homely illustration of what the situation actually is. We have ministers apparently living like hermits within their own departments, thinking only of the immediate problems that come to those departments. There seems to be a lack of over-all review of the situation and a lack of co-ordination, so that the efforts of one department will not create problems in another.
A moment ago I mentioned the problem in connection with our growing cities. As far as I can see there is no conscious endeavour by the government to curtail or to direct in a different direction the tendency of our
Supply-National Defence large metropolitan areas to grow even larger. To me, if an atomic war should ever occur this is a problem of major importance. I think it is fair to say that at the present time there is no means of defending large cities 100 per cent against atomic attack, even against aircraft let alone against other means such as the intermediate range ballistic missile or the intercontinental ballistic missile of the future.
I think perhaps there is a tendency to take large cities for granted. Not only is there that tendency, but there is a tendency to brag about the fact that our cities are growing larger all the time and are surpassing other cities in population, area and that sort of thing. To me that sort of thing is something like a hypochondriac boasting about the magnitude of his ailments. Cities now are obsolete.
Cities were first created for three principal reasons. It was necessary that they be congested because a wall had to be put around them for defence. Second, in previous ages communication was a great problem and could be accomplished only by sending a messenger from one person to another. Third, there was the problem of transportation.
In this day and age of instantaneous communication cities are not justified on those grounds. On the ground of transportation they are not justified, because our cities now have become so large and congested that we are obliged to tunnel through the earth to get from one place to another, and it is impossible to find a place to park in most of them. Then in the third place, from the point of view of defence modern cities are a detriment and a handicap rather than an asset because, as our cities grow larger, a larger and larger percentage of our population and of our potential production can be knocked out by a minimum number of atomic bombs. It is therefore my belief that large cities, perhaps even cities over 50,000 in population, are as obsolete as are medieval castles in this day and age.
I feel that we have here a huge problem- an elephantine problem,-as I said before. I feel it is one that must be attacked with a brave new way of thinking, with the realization that progress is not something that just happens by accident and is not something that is inevitable, but that it is something that must be brought about by hard work, conscience and sound thinking. We as a nation at this time need real, inspired, and dedicated leadership. We require men of great ability to find the thread that leads to progress in the tangled skein of problems that are before us at the present time.

The lack of such leadership has left us like babes in the woods, like children lost in the countryside, not knowing what direction will lead to escape. Sometimes we wander in the direction of progress and sometimes we wander by accident in the way of retrogression, thinking that we escape. Real leadership can correct that situation.
Speaking of babes in the woods reminds me that I used to notice, in England during the last war, that when one was on the ground one had the impression that the landscape of England was very confused and irregular, and that every landmark led to nowhere in particular. But those who flew over England found that once you got up above the tangle of the situation you realized that there were straight lines radiating in all directions across England, especially from the old Roman camps, and that those lines were made up perhaps of a road here or a mark of a different colour across a field or something of that sort. That is the sort of situation we are in at the present time. We need leadership that will see the whole problem and coordinate our effort in one direction so we can make progress, and so the progress will be real, not something that is painted as progress but which in actual fact may be retrogression.
I think at the present time there is a real necessity for all leaders in all fields in this country to have a real appreciation of the problem before us. It is no longer something that can be left as a problem to be met only by professional soldiers. The problem is wider than that. As a step in this direction I should like to see set up in this country a defence college to which leaders in all phases of life would go in order to get an appreciation of what the problem is. Such a plan should include leaders in industry as well as our top-ranking military men. It should include political leaders and our top scientists. The problem of survival is a complicated one that involves all these fields.
If we are trying to look into the future and see what are the immediate possibilities, we can see that there are a number that are open to us. By some happy combination of chance we might in the near future embark upon a future of real peace. If that were the case, defence would become a secondary problem. But as far as I can see at the moment there does not seem to be any likelihood of that happening in the immediate future. We may find ourselves engaged in a period of small wars like the Korean war and others. Only in such a situation would our present defence efforts meet the problem because, generally speaking, our defence concept is based on former wars rather than on what

may occur in the future, although I grant that in many directions attempts are being made to meet the problems that may arise in the future.
Then of course we may be obliged to live through a prolonged period of cold war during which we will have to spend large amounts on national defence. If we fail to meet that threat it is not because we are not spending large amounts of treasure and great amounts of energy and endeavour in national defence. For example, this year it is proposed that we spend $1,804 million on defence; that includes defence production and civil defence. This amount is 37 per cent of our national budget and about 7 per cent of our gross national product. Hence if we fail to survive it will not be because we have not spent enough money. But on the other hand we should realize that the spending of money alone will not guarantee survival.
There are many lessons to be learned from history in that regard. Only recently the French nation spent vast sums to build the Maginot line. Further back in history you have similar examples. It was not lack of endeavour or lack of funds that prevented them from defending themselves when the war came. In a condition of prolonged cold war, in our very effort to defend ourselves we may defeat our ends. We may lose some of our liberties; we may strain our resources in other directions so we cannot compete commercially in world markets and our economy will suffer. I think it was Nietzsche, the famous German philosopher of the last century, who said that simply by being compelled to keep constantly on his guard a man may grow so weary as to be unable any longer to defend himself. There is a real danger that the western world in general might find itself in that position if the cold war continues.
Then there is the theory, of course, that we can dispense with most of our expensive defences of a conventional nature and bank everything on massive retaliation, and in that way scare any potential enemy out of attack on us. This, in my opinion, is a dangerous gamble at best. It is only a type of Russian roulette, and some day if that is continued, though it may be justified on a short-term basis, someone is going to pull the trigger and have his brains blown out. If that should happen we would be engaged in a full scale atomic war, something that is more horrible to contemplate than the average person realizes.
There is a tendency for humans generally,
I suppose, to have a blind faith that this cannot happen to them. Most of the peoples of the past who fell into tragedy and were

eliminated believed it could not happen to them. They lived on in blissful ignorance until the catastrophe was upon them. There are those people who feel that a full scale atomic war would be too horrible to contemplate and therefore it cannot happen. If we look at history at all it does not show that just because a thing is horrible it will not happen.
I am not one who tends to give much credence to prophecy; nevertheless I would not be so callous as to suggest that such a thing is impossible. If one reads through Tennyson's "Locksley Hall", which was written about 115 years ago, he will be struck by the accuracy of some of the prophecies there. For instance, one verse reads:
When I dipt into the future far as human eye could see;
Saw the vision of the world, and all the wonder that would be.
Saw the heavens fill with commerce, argosies of magic sails,
Pilots of the purple twilight, dropping down with costly bales;
We in our lifetime have seen that prophecy fulfilled, not only in general outline but even to the extent of the way in which it is presented.

There are optimistic parts, but I am going to give the next verse which is not an optimistic one, and if it proves to be true it is something rather horrible to contemplate. This verse reads:
Heard the heavens fill with shouting, and there rain'd a ghastly dew
From the nations' airy navies grappling in the central blue;
I am not suggesting that the policy of the defence department should be based on Tennyson's poems or anything of that sort. Nevertheless that lays before us a picture of what may be in store for us. A responsible senior officer of the United States recently gave evidence before a committee of the United States Senate, and estimated that in a full scale atomic attack on Russia as many as 800 million lives might be wiped out, depending on the direction of the wind. Most people do not realize that the hydrogen bomb is measured in megatons, the equivalent of a million tons of T.N.T. A modern hydrogen bomb could wipe out a city entirely, leaving nothing in its place but a huge crater. In addition there would be great destruction from atomic fall-out for a long distance down wind. Those of us who live in the extremities of the country have concern and pity for the people who are forced to live in the large urban areas of this country for many 67509-390
Supply-National Defence reasons, and that is only one of them. If we wanted to be selfish about it, I do not think I could imagine anything less desirable than to have atomic fall-out land on my farm which consisted of the debris of and ashes of the inhabitants of a city like Toronto; but it is something that would be a reality if full scale atomic war were to come about.
There is a tendency for us to take a narrow view of things, not only so far as the general concept of the problem is concerned but to put a special importance on the small period of time in which we happen to be living. We are in the position that we have very little knowledge of the life of the earth except for a small period of recorded history. We are in the position of the weaver who can only see the last thread in the carpet in the loom. We would appreciate our own insignificance if we were in a position to unroll the carpet and see the full pattern from which we might be able to determine where we go from here. We should realize that for vast eons of time before man was ever seen on the earth, life went on in the form of lower animals and insects.
It is believed, as a matter of fact, that for a long period of time insect life was the major form of life on the earth and that a higher form did not evolve at that time because radioactivity was still so intense the higher forms of life could not survive. It is a scientific fact that insects can stand a much higher concentration of radioactivity than the higher forms of life. It may well be that if a full scale atomic war should ever come the results may be more devastating than we even care to contemplate. But the fact that that is so will not prevent it. As a matter of fact, it could well be that after such a war the human species might be found only in remote islands in the Pacific or down around Cape Horn, or somewhere like that.
Of course, I have been asked to look at the optimistic side, and there is a long-range optimistic thing about this. That is that radioactivity also causes an acceleration in evolution by mutation, and after a long period of this, after a full-scale atomic war, it might be that a more intelligent form of human being might evolve, a form of human being that could find the means of solving the problems that to us have been so insurmountable, a type of human being that could even learn to find a way whereby nations could live in peace with each other. To satisfy the hon. member who interrupted I shall quote, though I did not intend to, a more optimistic verse from the same poem:
There the common sense of most shall hold a fretful realm in awe,
And the kindly earth shall slumber, lapt in universal law.

Supply-National Defence That is desirable, no doubt, but I should like to think there is a more direct way of achieving it that we do not have; that even not we have arrived at the position where we shall learn, without having to learn the hard way, because the hard ways to learn are getting harder all the time and more destructive all the time, and the chances of survival are becoming less and less.
I would like to think that we can have some real leadership in this problem of defence, this problem of survival, and that some attention will be given to those wider aspects of the whole problem. I have avoided, and intentionally avoided, speaking about the particular problems of the minister's department at this time, but I may talk about some of them as the individual items are called. I make no apology for that, because I believe it is good once in a while to stop looking at the individual trees and stand back and try to have some conception of what the whole forest looks like. Only by that process can we meet these problems that the human race has never met before, has never been confronted with before; problems that cannot be solved by old methods, problems that require decisive action, the best brains available and concerted dedication to their solution. Only if that comes about can we hope to suggest that Tennyson was justified when he said: Yet I doubt not thro' the ages one increasing purpose runs,
And the thoughts of men are widen'd with the process of the suns.

Mr. Chairman, it is not my intention to delay the committee but I do think a number of things have been said in the debate this afternoon that call for some comment. The hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings and the hon. member for Kamloops and others have spoken of the danger of our defence planning taking on the aspect of a "stockade mentality", which was the term used by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings. This arises out of the very large expenditures and the very great and extraordinary efforts that over the past few years have gone into the construction of the radar warning lines that are now taking shape in Canada's northland.
Of course the question of one's mentality and one's approach to these things is a matter of individual responsibility, and I cannot speak for the hon. members who have expressed this view. All I can say is that I have not been able to find in anybody with whom I have discussed these things in the defence department or in the other departments of government that are dealing with them, or among the public, anything that 
indicates that there is any kind of a "stockade mentality". I think these early warning and other warning lines are properly understood and their function is quite reasonably well appreciated. They are what the term implies, warning lines.
The hon. members opposite who speak on matters of defence generally have some experience in one or other of the armed services, and I am sure they know and realize that in military matters the most important and the most essential thing is to know where your enemy is and what he is doing. In modern warfare, in a situation where we must foresee and where we may be faced with the possibility of aerial attack over the vast uninhabitated northern areas of Canada, I cannot imagine any other way in which the essential information of where our enemy is and to where he is going can be secured except by using these modern developments of radar and electronic communication to get that essential information.
Nobody believes that simply getting that information is any defence, any more than to pick up a spyglass and see the armada coming over the horizon in the English channel was any defence against the armada in that day. It is a matter of getting the information about your enemy's movements in the best and the quickest way possible and getting it when the enemy is as far away from his objective as is possible, and then communicating that information to the vital defence centres and taking the necessary remedial action.
If the expenditures that are being made and the very extraordinary efforts that have been put out by the contractors and the people who have been working on these lines are going to be misunderstood and represented purely as building up a Maginot line across the northern part of this country, I think a good deal of the value of these things will be wasted. I believe it would be well for all hon. members of this house to take a more realistic and more fundamental approach to these problems.
Most of the hon. members who have spoken in the debate this afternoon have, in one way or another, repeated the suggestion which has been heard so often inside this house and outside of it that there is a lack of information in this country about defence. Before we take this repeated assertion as proof we should look for a moment at the information that is available, not only to our members but to the Canadian public generally, and see just what are the facts.
First of all, the basic facts of national defence are very easily available to all hon. members and to members of the general

public. In the first place there is the annual report of the department. That is a publication which is simply crammed with facts about national defence, about the three services, about what has gone on during the year and about the general policies which are being followed by the department and the success that is being achieved in meeting the defence objectives we have set up.
Then there is the white paper which is prepared by the department and tabled in the house annually by the minister prior to consideration of the defence estimates. That is also a publication that is put out to explain the basic policies of the department, outlining the particular achievements which have been realized during the year and setting out tables showing the strength of the forces and detailed information of that kind which is thus available to the house and the public.
In connection with matters of policy within the department and of defence policy more generally in the international sphere there are statements made from time to time in the house by the Minister of National Defence, by the Secretary of State for External Affairs and by the Prime Minister which clearly set out the matters with which the department is dealing, our relations with our NATO allies, the projects that we undertake either in general association with other NATO countries or in special association either with the United States, the United Kingdom or another of our allies and related subjects of that kind.
Then concerning the question of expenditures there are 110 pages of details of the expenditures of the Department of National Defence in the public accounts this year. Every year a similar number of pages, which are very closely printed and full ot facts, are contained in that document which is readily available. In the book of estimates that is before the committee at the present time there are over 40 pages of details of the expenditures which we are presently considering.
Finally, the Minister of National Defence and other ministers concerned with the more general aspects of defence are in the house every day the house is sitting and are subject to questioning by hon. members opposite.
The hon. member for Kamloops raised a question about security and the denial of information on that basis, and the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke raised very briefly the same problem. It is a problem. I am sure nobody claims that any system of security can be perfect. I am equally sure no one claims it is possible by classifying a particular project or subject and saying that information relating to

Supply-National Defence it cannot be published can in every case prevent information getting out into the public domain that is either helpful to potential enemies or which is capable of being helpful to them.
Surely, Mr. Chairman, all hon. members must agree that a department dealing with so many matters which are of a secret nature of which the confidential nature must be kept through some system of security, must lay down some rules which the department itself must to the best of its ability respect, not only in our own national interest but also in the light of our duty to keep faith with our allies, who share very confidential information with us in the belief that we will make a reasonable effort to see that such information is treated with the confidence it deserves. That is all that is implied in those rare and unusual cases when it is said in this house, in committee or some other place that information on a certain subject must be denied publication because of the consideration of security.
In addition to what I have already said, Mr. Chairman, it is a matter of common knowledge to everybody in the country that Canadian newspapers, newsreels and radio and television programs contain a great mass of information about our armed forces and about what is taking place in matters of defence.
Many hon. members of this house during the last few sessions alone have visited radar stations of the kind referred to by the hon. member for Kamloops, and have visited air stations and the defence centre at St. Hubert, for example. They have visited army camps, naval depots and ships as well. In other words the integral parts of our defence set-up and of the three services are open for inspection.
It may be that some particular development of a confidential nature with respect to armaments or something of that kind may have to be kept confidential, but one might say that 99 per cent of these installations are open for inspection, and the greatest facilities are given by the minister and the department for members of parliament-and at times when it can be arranged for members of the public-to visit these places and see for themselves what is going on and understand as best they can what our defence system comprises.
Let me review very briefly what are the main facts about Canadian defence that are so well known. First of all it is well known that we have an air division and an army brigade in Europe. At least 20 hon. members of this house in the last few years have visited either or both units of the air division and

Supply-National Defence the army brigade. A number of hon. gentlemen have reported on their visits in this house, and I have yet to hear any hon. member report that he was not permitted to visit freely and was not given every facility for inspecting these overseas installations to see how things were going, to talk with the officers and men involved and to see their equipment and all that sort of thing. What more could be done to disclose to the members of this house and the Canadian public what we are doing in connection with our contribution to NATO? I think very little further can be done, and I have heard no suggestions as to exactly what more could be done.
We have three army brigades and a mobile striking force in Canada; that is well known. The camps at which the army units are stationed are known not only to hon. members of this house but to the public, and many people who are interested secure access to these army installations. They see what is going on. In many cases they have friends amongst the officers and men and they receive a great deal of information. Information of this nature is freely available to every hon. member of this house. Any hon. gentleman in this house can visit these locations, as I am sure many of them have done, and if they find anything they think is wrong or anything they think is not being done in accordance with proper policy they are free to bring it up in the house, either on the estimates or as a question on orders of the day.
Then with respect to the navy, in which I am particularly interested, we have two main and substantial naval installations located in Nova Scotia and another substantial installation on the west coast. These installations are on exactly the same basis as the army installations all over the country. People who are interested in what is going on can find out. Civilians work in these places along with service personnel, and there is no lack of information about the things being achieved in the naval installations.
We have 40 fighting ships serving on both coasts. While those ships are not generally open for inspection, they are open at regular times when the public are invited to come aboard. I know that quite often hon. members when on the east or west coast take advantage of the opportunity to visit these ships, and often go on short cruises at sea.
As far as the air force is concerned, it is well known that we have nine CF-100 squadrons in Canada on an operational basis and that altogether we have more than 3,000 aircraft which are operational. The R.C.A.F.

stations both at home and overseas are open in the same way as are the naval and army installations.
By reason of all this anyone who is really interested in our defence spending and policy can look around if he wishes to do so. On the basis alone of information that is so widely and generally available, any hon. member has ready access to much factual material, and if he desires additional information he can put questions or inform himself in any number of ways.
The hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings repeated and supported the suggestion made by the Leader of the Opposition with respect to the type of defence committee the Leader of the Opposition now thinks should be set up by this house to look into defence matters. Of course this is based on the incorrect assumption and repeated assertion that information on defence is not readily available. I submit that that is not correct, but in any event that is the basis of the request for a committee.
The hon. member went on to explain the kind of information he would like to get through such a committee. Actually most of the information is just as easily available when the estimates are being considered as it would be in such a committee.
However, it is interesting to look at the history of these requests by the Leader of the Opposition for committees on defence. Most hon. members will remember that in 1950 after the defence program got under way as a result of the Korean war the Leader of the Opposition started to ask for a committee on defence expenditures. The presumption then was that the very large amounts of money that were being spent on defence were being spent to a large extent improperly and wastefully. So the request was made for a committee on defence expenditure.
That request was considered by the government and was granted. My understanding of the matter is that the Leader of the Opposition was consulted with respect to the terms of reference to that committee, and that as a matter of fact those terms were drawn up in what he considered to be the proper wording in order to bring about the result he wanted in connection with the examination of defence expenditures.
That committee sat during three sessions. It sat first in the short session of the fall of 1951, when it held five meetings. But even then it received a tremendous amount of information which was asked for by members of the committee. The committee was set up again at the next session, that of 1952, under the same terms of reference. It held 17 meetings and received a correspondingly

greater mass of information on defence expenditures and defence matters which I do not think has been equalled by any other committee of this house and so far as I know not equalled by a similar committee anywhere else. Then the committee was set up again in 1953, and during that session held 26 meetings.
During the three sessions the committee held a total of 48 meetings and there are three volumes of the proceedings. The first one is rather small but the other two are quite substantial indeed. The way the committee operated was to ask the opposition members on the committee what features of defence expenditure they wanted to examine, and arrangements were made to examine those features in which they were most interested. You have only to refer to the minutes of proceedings to see the steps which were taken to consult with members of the opposition as to particular features at which they wanted to look. You can follow the proceedings right through and see how they were given every possible facility to question the officials who were dealing with the particular matters that they themselves had selected.
What was the result? The result was that the opposition members did not find what they thought they were going to find. They did not turn up the kind of mismanagement of defence expenditures and extravagance and the various things which they had stated in the debate before the committees were set up they were sure were there.

I submit that in reality this is the situation. Hon. members of the opposition are really searching around not for material on defence but for political material. That has been only too obvious in the past.
There has been some criticism about the armed forces in general. The point that should be emphasized in this debate is that anybody who has had occasion to look at the armed forces of Canada either at home or abroad has reported most favourably on the way in which those armed forces perform, their morale, their training and their general excellence. Some people who have made these statements-and I may say that I refer to members of this house-go on to say, in spite of this excellence that everything is wrong with the Department of National Defence. They say it is poorly organized, that the minister is not doing his job properly, that there are too many civilians hanging around, that they are not doing a good job, and direct these criticisms at the department.
How can a department which could be in any way described in the way hon. members describe the Department of National Defence possibly produce the excellent results that they admit are produced? It is the three armed services that are the real testimony to the organization of the Department of National Defence and the way the department is carrying out its purposes and its policies. I certainly am more than prepared to rest any defence that the minister and the department might need on the record of the three armed services of Canada, a record of which, I am sure, even hon. members opposite are proud.

speechtext:
I promise the committee that I shall not hold them as long as the previous speaker. It is not my purpose to deal in generalities with statements made by others

Supply-National Defence In this debate. I would agree with the statements by other members of this group with regard to charges, made by respected leaders, that have gone unanswered. As the minister said today, some of them were opinions and not facts, I feel that possibly we should have these men before a special committee set up for the purpose of discussing defence so we may arrive at our own conclusions as to whether they are opinions or facts. These men could answer the charges, and we could decide for ourselves.
The question I have in mind, however, is one of which I am not too sure the minister is completely aware. It has to do with the demoralizing effect on our civil service and casual employees of the Department of National Defence who are concerned with the labour pay question on the Pacific coast. I speak more specifically of the Chilliwack area.
The question I have in mind is that of rates of pay offered by the department for certain jobs as compared with the current rates of pay effective in the Chilliwack area. I am using as an illustration the rates for a certain project that was undertaken by the Department of National Defence on September 1, 1955, as compared with the current rates of pay in the Chilliwack area for the same jobs, effective on February 15, 1956. Whilst there is a slight discrepancy in the period, the minister will recognize that there is not enough difference in time to compensate for the difference in pay.
I begin by mentioning the wages paid to carpenters in each instance. The Department of National Defence pays $2.22 per hour for carpenters employed in the Chilliwack area, and the current rate of pay in the same area is $2.22 for other employees working at carpentering. Of course these two are comparable, and this is the only instance, I may say at this time, where the wages compare in any way.
Chauffeurs and truck drivers in the Department of National Defence are paid $1.45 per hour; in Chilliwack chauffeurs and truck drivers get $1.60 per hour. Heavy equipment operators in the Department of National Defence get $1.75 per hour; others working in the same area get $2.45 per hour. Those are men employed on drag line crane and bulldozer work. The ordinary labourer in the Department of National Defence gets $1.40; the labourer not working on defence projects gets $1.60. Plumbers' and steam-fitters' helpers in the Department of National Defence get $1.55, as opposed to $1.85. The plumbers and steamfitters themselves get $2.10 in the Department of National Defence; otherwise in civilian jobs they get $2.35 per hour.

Pipe layers, caulkers and solderers get $1.65. Pump operators get $1.82; that is the current rate paid in the Chilliwack area. Brush painters get $1.80 working for the Department of National Defence, as opposed to $2.16 for those working in civilian jobs. Those who work with spray guns at painting for the Department of National Defence get $1.90, as opposed to $2.26. Sheet metal workers get $2 per hour in the Department of National Defence as opposed to $2.35 in civilian jobs. Welders get $1.75 as compared with $2.
My time is limited, and I should like to finish if the committee would be kind enough to give me a few minutes more. I shall not be more than three or four minutes, you may rest assured, but I wish to point out this. The wages for carpenters in the Department of National Defence and for carpenters in civilian jobs are the same, but that is the top wage paid by the Department of National Defence for workers in that area. However, in civilian jobs, the bulldozer operator gets $2.45 as the top wage. The lowest wage paid by the Department of National Defence is $1.40 per hour, which is the wage for a common labourer, whilst in comparison truck drivers get $1.60, which is the lowest wage paid by private industry in the area.
My plea is that the rate of pay by the Department of National Defence should compare with the wages paid in the surrounding community, so we would not have this demoralizing effect upon the unions and upon the workers within the area itself. Those who are working as casual employees in the Department of National Defence are entitled to the same wages as those in other employment. I am sure the minister can understand that if his department is getting wage earners for a similar job in his department at from 20 to 30 cents per hour less than is paid in the civilian field, that is bound to have some effect upon the civilian employees as well as upon departmental employees. I think the government should set an example by maintaining wages in keeping with the wages in the communities themselves.

speechtext:
This morning the hon. member for Wentworth (Mr. Lennard) asked me, without notice, to say how soon I thought the report of the inquiry concerning criminal sexual psychopaths would be available. In a mistaken recollection of a conversation which I had had with my deputy before my recent illness I said that majority and minority reports were being prepared in connection with this inquiry. This is not correct. It is the other commission presided over by Chief Justice McRuer in which a minority report is in course of preparation.
I think it might be helpful for me to put on the record the present standing of both these commissions. The commissioners appointed to inquire into and report upon whether the criminal law of Canada relating to the defence of insanity should be amended in any respect and, if so, in what manner and to what extent, are Chief Justice McRuer of the high court of justice of Ontario; Dr. Gustave Desrochers, assistant superintendent
Criminal Law
of St. Michel's hospital at the city of Quebec; Her Honour Judge Helen Kinnear, county court judge of the county of Haldimand, Ontario; Dr. Robert O. Jones, professor of psychiatry at Dalhousie University, Halifax; and Joseph Harris, Esquire, president of the Great-West Life Assurance Company of Winnipeg.
The draft majority report of this commission is complete. The majority report will be presented later simultaneously with a minority report which is now in the course of preparation, unless in the meanwhile the differences of opinion between the majority and the minority can be resolved. We hope that the commission's report or reports will be available this autumn.
The commissioners to inquire into and report upon the question whether the criminal law of Canada relating to criminal sexual psychopaths should be amended in any respect and, if so, in what manner and to what extent, are the aforesaid Chief Justice McRuer, Dr. Gustave Desrochers and Her Honour Judge Helen Kinnear.
The hearings of this commission have been completed and on the basis of information which my deputy secured from Chief Justice McRuer this afternoon we hope that the report of the commission will be presented this autumn, but it will not be before September 15.
